title: Standalone Components
description: Standalone components, incremental migration, lazy route boundaries, provider scope, and bundle-safe architecture.

blocks.title: Standalone components in simple language
blocks.content:
A standalone component is an Angular component that manages its own template dependencies. If its template uses another component, directive, or pipe, that dependency is listed directly in the component's `imports` array.

A simple mental model: an NgModule is like one shared toolbox for a group of components. A standalone component carries a small list of the exact tools its own template needs.

Since Angular 19, components are standalone by default unless `standalone: false` is specified. Angular still supports NgModules for existing applications; standalone is recommended for new code, not the only valid mode.

Standalone changes where template dependencies are declared. It does not automatically create lazy loading, improve runtime speed, or remove architectural coupling. Lazy loading still requires a dynamic route boundary such as `loadComponent` or `loadChildren`.
keyPoints: Angular 19+ components are standalone by default; older components may explicitly use `standalone: false`.
`imports` controls what the template can use; `providers` controls dependency-injection scope.
Standalone and NgModule-based code can coexist during an incremental migration.
Standalone makes dependencies easier to see, but bundle improvement comes from correct lazy boundaries and import graphs.

blocks.title: How compilation, imports, and lazy loading fit together
blocks.content:
Angular reads component metadata at build time. The compiler uses the `imports` array to understand template symbols such as `AsyncPipe`, a child component, or a directive.

A normal TypeScript import is not automatically a template import. You may import a class at the top of the file for TypeScript and still need to list it in `@Component({ imports: [...] })` before using its selector or pipe in the template.

For lazy loading, the important boundary is the dynamic `import()` in the router. Code reachable only through that boundary can be placed in a lazy chunk or a shared lazy chunk. If the same feature is also imported synchronously from an eagerly loaded file—often through a broad barrel file—the feature can become part of the eager graph.

Providers also have lifetimes. A route provider is created for that route environment and can be destroyed when the route environment is destroyed. A component provider creates an instance for that component subtree. A root provider is normally shared application-wide.
keyPoints: Template dependencies and DI providers solve different problems.
`loadComponent` creates a lazy entry point; static imports determine what is reachable from it.
Bundlers may create shared chunks, so “everything goes into one route file” is not guaranteed.
Provider placement must match ownership of state and side effects.

blocks.title: Practical standalone route with feature-scoped state
blocks.explanation: The route is the code-splitting boundary, while the route-level `OrdersStore` owns state only for the feature lifetime. The component imports only the template dependencies it actually uses.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why did Angular introduce standalone APIs if NgModules already worked?
blocks.answer:
Standalone APIs remove an indirection layer. A component can declare its template dependencies directly, routes can lazy-load a component without a feature NgModule, and application providers can be configured through `ApplicationConfig`.

The deeper reason is maintainability: dependency ownership becomes local and easier for tools to analyze. However, standalone does not mean “no architecture.” Large applications still need clear feature boundaries, public APIs, provider scopes, and rules that prevent cross-feature imports.
blocks.explanation: A senior answer should explain both the developer-experience benefit and the remaining architecture responsibilities. Saying only “less boilerplate” is correct but incomplete.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does importing a standalone component automatically make it lazy?
blocks.answer:
No. A component becomes lazy only when it is reachable through a dynamic import boundary, such as a router `loadComponent` callback or another runtime `import()`.

Adding a component to another eagerly loaded component's `imports` array is still a static dependency and normally makes it reachable from the eager bundle graph.
blocks.explanation: Standalone controls declaration and composition. Lazy loading is a bundler/router concern based on dynamic imports.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A large Angular application has NgModules, circular dependencies, and active production delivery. How would you migrate without a big-bang rewrite?
blocks.answer:
1. Establish a baseline: production build size, initial route size, route-load time, test status, and known circular dependencies.
2. Map feature dependencies and start with leaf routes or isolated shared components, not the root module.
3. Run Angular's standalone migration schematic in small paths. Commit each migration step separately and manually review generated imports.
4. Keep module-based and standalone areas interoperating while migration is in progress.
5. Move routing to `loadComponent` or lazy `loadChildren` at business-feature boundaries. Do not assume conversion alone creates lazy chunks.
6. Replace broad shared or global-import modules with focused imports or small purpose-built UI libraries. Avoid barrels that re-export feature internals.
7. Review provider scope carefully. Moving a service from a module to a route or component can create additional instances, reset state unexpectedly, or duplicate WebSockets and caches.
8. Verify forms, dialogs, dynamic components, content projection, tests, SSR/hydration, and third-party libraries after each slice.
9. Add dependency-boundary lint rules and bundle budgets so the old coupling does not return.
10. Roll out route by route with rollback-ready commits and compare the same metrics after every release.
blocks.explanation: This approach treats migration as dependency and lifecycle work, not a mechanical decorator change.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Creating one enormous `SHARED_IMPORTS` or global imports array and adding it to every standalone component.
blocks.whyItHappens: It feels similar to the old SharedModule and reduces typing, but it hides dependencies, can pull unnecessary code into many chunks, and can recreate circular coupling.
blocks.correctApproach: Use direct imports for feature code. A small, reviewed group of stable design-system primitives can be acceptable, but measure bundle impact and avoid exporting feature internals.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Judge a standalone migration by dependency clarity, provider correctness, lazy-chunk behavior, and delivery risk—not by the number of deleted NgModules.
keyPoints: Use `ng generate @angular/core:standalone` incrementally and verify after every mode.
Inspect source maps or bundle reports for accidental eager imports and duplicated libraries.
Test whether route/component-scoped services are created and destroyed at the intended time.
Keep feature public APIs small and prohibit imports from another feature's internal folders.
Compare initial bundle, route chunk, route activation time, and production errors before and after.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Standalone is the default authoring model, but NgModules remain supported for legacy code.
- Direct template imports improve clarity; dynamic imports create lazy boundaries.
- Provider scope is part of the migration and can change state lifetime.
- A migration should be incremental, measurable, and reversible.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/components
- https://angular.dev/guide/ngmodules/overview
- https://angular.dev/reference/migrations/standalone
- https://angular.dev/guide/routing/define-routes

title: Lifecycle Hooks
description: Component lifecycle timing, render callbacks, resource ownership, cleanup, and memory-leak diagnosis.

blocks.title: Lifecycle hooks as ownership checkpoints
keyPoints: The first `ngOnChanges` runs before `ngOnInit` when the component has bound inputs.
`ngOnInit` runs before the component's own template is fully initialized.
View-query or DOM-dependent work belongs after view initialization or a render callback.
Render callbacks do not run during SSR or build-time pre-rendering.
Cleanup should follow ownership: the code that creates a resource should define how it is released.

blocks.title: DestroyRef and modern cleanup
blocks.content:
`DestroyRef` lets cleanup stay near setup instead of forcing every resource into one large `ngOnDestroy` method. Angular's `takeUntilDestroyed()` operator completes an observable when the current injection context is destroyed.

Not every observable requires manual unsubscription. `HttpClient` observables normally complete after one response, and `AsyncPipe` manages its own subscription. Long-lived streams, global events, timers, observers, sockets, and third-party widget instances do require a clear lifetime.

A memory leak is not simply “a subscription exists.” A leak occurs when something with a longer lifetime retains a component, DOM node, large data structure, or resource after the feature should be gone.
keyPoints: Prefer `AsyncPipe`, signals, or `takeUntilDestroyed()` over hand-written `Subject<void>` boilerplate.
Explicitly destroy chart/editor/map instances that register global resources.
Root services intentionally outlive routes; do not store route-component references in them.
Use heap snapshots and repeated-navigation tests to prove retention rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Resource setup and cleanup kept together
blocks.explanation: The chart is created only after the DOM render and both the observer and chart are released with the owning component. Remember that `afterNextRender` does not execute during server rendering.

blocks.title: Lifecycle order question
blocks.question: A parent binds an input to a child component. Which runs first in the child: the first `ngOnChanges` or `ngOnInit`?
blocks.answer: `ngOnChanges` runs first, followed by `ngOnInit`.
blocks.explanation: Angular first provides initial input values and reports them through `ngOnChanges`; then one-time initialization runs in `ngOnInit`.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What belongs in the constructor, `ngOnInit`, `ngAfterViewInit`, and `ngOnDestroy`?
blocks.answer:
Use the constructor mainly for dependency injection and setup that does not depend on initialized inputs or DOM.

Use `ngOnInit` for one-time initialization based on initial inputs or services. Use `ngAfterViewInit` when logic needs view children or the initialized view, but prefer `afterNextRender` for manual DOM writes/reads that should happen after rendering. Use `ngOnDestroy` or `DestroyRef` for timers, global listeners, observers, sockets, subscriptions, and third-party instances owned by the component.
blocks.explanation: The important idea is not memorizing hook names; it is choosing the first safe point and matching setup with cleanup.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Memory increases every time users navigate to and from a chart route. How do you investigate and fix it?
blocks.answer:
First reproduce the issue with a production build and a scripted navigation loop. Record a baseline heap snapshot, navigate 20–30 times, force garbage collection in the profiling environment, and compare snapshots.

Inspect retained component instances, detached DOM nodes, chart objects, `ResizeObserver`/`MutationObserver`, window/document listeners, timers, WebSocket subscriptions, and closures capturing large datasets. Use the retaining path to find the actual long-lived owner.

Typical fixes are: destroy the chart instance, disconnect observers, remove global listeners, use `takeUntilDestroyed()` for long-lived streams, bound or reset `shareReplay` caches, and avoid keeping component callbacks in root services or static collections.

Then repeat the exact navigation script. The retained instance count should return near the baseline and memory should plateau rather than rise linearly. Add an end-to-end stress test or diagnostic check for the regression.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer starts with measurement and retaining paths, not “unsubscribe from everything.”

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Calling expensive calculations or mutating component state inside `ngAfterViewChecked` or `ngDoCheck`.
blocks.whyItHappens: These hooks can run many times, so work is repeated and a mutation during traversal can schedule another check or cause an expression-changed error.
blocks.correctApproach: Move pure derived state to `computed`, memoized selectors, or input transforms. Use explicit events/effects for side effects, and render callbacks only for real DOM integration.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Use lifecycle hooks only when the lifecycle itself is the requirement. A normal method, computed value, signal, template binding, or RxJS pipeline is often clearer.
keyPoints: Keep constructors free of uncontrolled network calls and DOM assumptions.
Avoid manual subscriptions when `AsyncPipe` or `toSignal` expresses the ownership better.
Use `DestroyRef.destroyed` before delayed work if code may run after destruction.
Profile retained objects after repeated create/destroy cycles.
Test SSR separately when using browser-only APIs or render callbacks.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Constructor creates the instance; hooks mark safe lifecycle checkpoints.
- Frequent checked hooks are not general event handlers.
- Use `DestroyRef` and lifecycle-bound utilities for cleanup.
- Prove memory leaks with retained-object analysis and repeatable navigation.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/components/lifecycle
- https://angular.dev/api/core/DestroyRef
- https://angular.dev/api/core/rxjs-interop/takeUntilDestroyed

title: Dependency Injection
description: Angular hierarchical DI, provider recipes, service responsibility, instance lifetime, and production scope bugs.

blocks.title: Dependency injection in simple language
keyPoints: The token identifies what is requested; the provider explains how to create or obtain it.
The nearest provider shadows providers for the same token higher in the hierarchy.
`InjectionToken` represents runtime values or interfaces because TypeScript interfaces disappear at runtime.
Provider scope must match the owner of state, caches, sockets, and side effects.

blocks.title: Provider recipes and resolution modifiers
blocks.content:
Angular providers can use `useClass`, `useValue`, `useFactory`, or `useExisting`.

- `useClass` selects an implementation.
- `useValue` supplies configuration or an already-created value.
- `useFactory` creates a value using runtime conditions or other injected dependencies.
- `useExisting` creates an alias to the same existing instance; it does not create a second object.

Resolution modifiers narrow or change lookup:
- `self`: only the current injector;
- `skipSelf`: begin at the parent;
- `optional`: return `null` instead of throwing when missing;
- `host`: stop at the host boundary.

Use these modifiers when the component contract genuinely requires a local or parent collaborator. Overusing them can make dependency behavior hard to understand.
keyPoints: `providedIn: "root"` is the normal tree-shakable choice for shared services.
Route providers are useful when state should reset when leaving a feature.
Component providers create isolated state but can accidentally duplicate expensive infrastructure.
Constructor injection and `inject()` use the same DI system; `inject()` requires an injection context.

blocks.title: Runtime abstraction with InjectionToken
blocks.explanation: The domain service depends on runtime abstractions instead of concrete construction. `useExisting` aliases the audit token to the same adapter instance, and the observable contract keeps completion and error handling explicit.

blocks.title: Instance question
blocks.question: Two sibling components each list `CartStore` in their own `providers` array. Do they share the same cart?
blocks.answer: No. Each sibling has a different element injector and receives its own `CartStore` instance. Their descendants share the instance belonging to their own sibling subtree unless a closer provider shadows it.
blocks.explanation: Provider location defines instance lifetime and visibility. The service class itself does not determine singleton behavior.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What is the purpose of Angular services, and why does Angular use dependency injection?
blocks.answer:
A service is appropriate when behavior or state has a cohesive responsibility outside one view—for example API access, authentication, feature state, calculations, logging, or workflow orchestration.

DI lets consumers request those collaborators without constructing them. This lowers coupling, supports test fakes and environment-specific implementations, centralizes configuration, and controls instance lifetime. I would still keep services focused: a service should expose a clear contract, not become a global dumping ground for unrelated functions and mutable state.
blocks.explanation: The best answer connects services to responsibility and DI to construction, substitution, and lifecycle—not simply “code reuse.”

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A stateful service is provided in root, a lazy route, and one child component. Users see inconsistent values and duplicate WebSocket connections. Explain the bug and redesign it.
blocks.explanation: The fix is not “always use root.” It is matching provider scope to ownership and separating responsibilities with different lifetimes.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Marking every class `providedIn: "root"` or providing the same service at several levels without an explicit lifetime decision.
blocks.whyItHappens: Root feels convenient and component providers feel isolated, but stateful services, caches, refresh logic, and sockets behave differently when multiple instances exist.
blocks.correctApproach: Document ownership, choose one provider boundary, split services whose responsibilities need different lifetimes, and test instance identity and teardown.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Use DI at real application boundaries: infrastructure, configuration, replaceable strategies, state ownership, and test seams. Keep small pure transformations as normal functions.
keyPoints: Keep constructors and provider factories lightweight; start side effects through explicit methods.
Use typed `InjectionToken`s for non-class values and runtime abstractions.
Avoid circular service dependencies; introduce a smaller contract or orchestrator instead.
Test root, route, and component provider behavior through navigation and destruction.
Verify that production optimizers can tree-shake unused root-provided services.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- DI separates construction from use.
- Angular resolves the nearest provider through element and environment injector hierarchies.
- Scope is a lifecycle decision, not only a syntax choice.
- Use tokens for runtime abstractions and configuration.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/di
- https://angular.dev/guide/di/hierarchical-dependency-injection
- https://angular.dev/guide/di/defining-dependency-providers
- https://angular.dev/api/core/InjectionToken

title: Change Detection
description: Angular 22 OnPush-default rendering, zoneless notifications, change-detection boundaries, and evidence-based optimization.

blocks.title: What change detection actually does
blocks.content:
Change detection is Angular's process for deciding which views need to be refreshed and then updating bindings in those views.

In Angular 22, `OnPush` is the default component strategy. `ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager`—with `Default` kept as its equivalent/deprecated name—is the opt-in strategy that checks a component whenever an application-wide synchronization reaches it.

An OnPush view becomes eligible for checking when Angular receives a notification such as a changed template-bound input, an event handled in its subtree, a signal read by the template changing, `AsyncPipe` marking the view, `markForCheck()`, or a component input being set through Angular APIs.

OnPush does not mean a component renders only once. It means Angular can skip the subtree when it has no relevant notification. It also does not make expensive template work cheap; if the view is checked, every binding in that view still needs evaluation.
keyPoints: OnPush is the default for components in Angular 22.
Signal writes notify Angular only for consumers that actually read the signal.
Stable references and granular state help Angular skip work; deep mutation can hide changes at boundaries.
Performance problems can also come from JavaScript, layout, paint, DOM size, network, and third-party libraries—not only change detection.

blocks.title: Zoneless Angular and explicit notifications
blocks.content:
Zoneless change detection is the default in Angular 21 and later. A new Angular 22 application does not need `provideZonelessChangeDetection()` unless code is being written for an older version or a test configuration. Adding `provideZoneChangeDetection()` explicitly opts an application back into ZoneJS-based scheduling.

Without ZoneJS, Angular does not use every timer or asynchronous callback as a reason to synchronize the application. State must change through Angular-aware notifications such as signals, template/host listeners, `AsyncPipe`, `ComponentRef.setInput`, or `markForCheck()`.

This is more predictable and often avoids unnecessary application-wide work, but legacy code that mutates plain fields inside arbitrary callbacks may not refresh. The solution is not to call `detectChanges()` everywhere. Prefer signals or observable/template bindings, and use `markForCheck()` for imperative integration.

Reactive-form model methods emit form observables but do not always schedule a component check in zoneless mode; connect relevant form state to a signal/observable consumed by the template or explicitly mark the view.
keyPoints: Zoneless is already the default in Angular 22.
`NgZone.run()` is not the main notification mechanism in zoneless applications.
Use `markForCheck()` to schedule a normal update; reserve `detectChanges()` for controlled local cases.
Test asynchronous updates without masking missing notifications through unconditional `fixture.detectChanges()`.

blocks.title: Granular signal state with OnPush-default rendering
blocks.explanation: The HTTP observable completes after the response, and writing the signal explicitly notifies the template consumers in a zoneless application. Computed values recalculate only when their tracked order changes.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Explain OnPush versus Eager/Default change detection in Angular 22.
blocks.answer:
OnPush is the Angular 22 default. Angular can skip an OnPush subtree until it receives a relevant notification—for example a changed bound input, an event in the subtree, a template-read signal update, `AsyncPipe`, or `markForCheck()`.

Eager/Default makes the component checked whenever Angular performs an application synchronization that reaches it. Eager can be useful for legacy components that mutate fields without explicit notifications, but it increases the amount of work Angular must consider.

I would not select a strategy only by convention. I would keep state flow explicit and measure real rendering cost with Angular DevTools and browser traces.
blocks.explanation: This updates the traditional interview answer: OnPush is no longer merely an optional optimization in new Angular 22 components; it is the default behavior.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: A third-party callback changes a plain class field, but the zoneless Angular 22 view does not update. Should you wrap it in `ngZone.run()`?
blocks.answer:
Not as the primary fix. In a zoneless application, re-entering `NgZone` is not what schedules rendering. Update a signal read by the template, emit through an observable consumed by `AsyncPipe`, or call `ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()` after updating the field.

`NgZone.run()` and `runOutsideAngular()` remain compatible mainly for libraries that also support ZoneJS applications, but Angular-aware notifications are the reliable cross-mode mechanism.
blocks.explanation: The original ZoneJS mental model is outdated for default Angular 22 applications.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A dashboard with 80 widgets becomes slow whenever one global filter changes. How would you diagnose and optimize it?
blocks.answer:
1. Reproduce the exact interaction in a production build and record Angular DevTools plus Chrome Performance traces.
2. Separate costs: API/network, RxJS processing, JavaScript calculations, view checks, DOM updates, layout/paint, charts, and memory pressure.
3. Inspect the state graph. A single broad store emission or selector returning fresh objects can invalidate every widget even when most data is unchanged.
4. Give each widget a narrow signal or selector for only the data it needs. Preserve stable references for unchanged slices.
5. Move template calculations into `computed()` or memoized selectors and keep them pure.
6. Use stable `track` expressions for repeated rows and reduce DOM with virtualization or conditional/deferred rendering.
7. Batch high-frequency data at a user-perceivable frame rate and avoid rendering every backend event.
8. Isolate heavy charts/editors, destroy inactive instances, and move CPU-only aggregation to a Web Worker or server when justified.
9. Make one change at a time and compare interaction latency, long tasks, view checks, DOM nodes, and memory.
10. Add a performance budget and repeatable benchmark to CI or release validation.
blocks.explanation: The senior approach begins with evidence and state granularity. Adding OnPush blindly is insufficient because it is already the default in Angular 22.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Calling `detectChanges()` after every callback or marking the root component for check whenever any data changes.
blocks.whyItHappens: It appears to fix stale UI quickly, but it hides missing state ownership and turns a local notification problem into repeated broad rendering work.
blocks.correctApproach: Use signals or narrow observable view models, call `markForCheck()` only at imperative boundaries, and profile the exact subtree and work that changes.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Optimize the state-to-view path before changing framework configuration. The goal is fewer invalidated consumers and less work per rendered view.
keyPoints: Use Angular DevTools and Chrome Performance together; component checks are only one part of rendering cost.
Prefer pure `computed()` values and stable references over template methods that allocate objects.
Use `@for (...; track item.id)` and virtualization for large collections.
In zoneless tests, use `await fixture.whenStable()` where practical to expose missing notifications.
Measure INP/interaction latency, long tasks, rendered node count, memory, and route-level telemetry.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- OnPush is the default in Angular 22; Eager/Default is opt-in.
- Zoneless is the default in Angular 21+ and relies on explicit Angular notifications.
- Signals, AsyncPipe, events, and markForCheck notify Angular.
- Profile state invalidation, JavaScript, DOM, layout, and paint before optimizing.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/components/advanced-configuration
- https://angular.dev/best-practices/skipping-subtrees
- https://angular.dev/guide/zoneless
- https://angular.dev/tools/devtools

title: Signals
description: Angular signals, computed state, effects, RxJS interop, equality, cleanup, and scalable store design.

blocks.title: Signals in simple language
blocks.content:
A signal is a value container that tells Angular which consumers use it and when its value changes. You read a signal by calling it, write a writable signal with `set()` or `update()`, and expose read-only state with `asReadonly()`.

A helpful mental model:
- `signal()` is source state;
- `computed()` is a spreadsheet formula derived from source state;
- `effect()` is a bridge to an external side effect such as local storage, analytics, a chart, or another imperative API.

Computed values are lazy and memoized. Angular tracks only the signals read during the latest computation, so dependencies can change dynamically.

Effects run at least once and are scheduled asynchronously as part of Angular synchronization. They should be the last reactive API you reach for. Do not use an effect to copy one signal into another when a computed or a better source-of-truth design can express the relationship.
keyPoints: Signals provide synchronous current values and dependency tracking.
Computed is for pure derived state; effect is for real side effects.
Signals use `Object.is()` equality by default, so mutating an object in place may not notify consumers.
Dependencies are tracked dynamically based on reads in the latest execution.

blocks.title: Signals and RxJS solve different problems
blocks.content:
Signals are excellent for synchronous application state and template-facing derived values. RxJS is excellent for streams over time: cancellation, retries, debouncing, concurrency, WebSockets, and combining asynchronous sources.

Use `toObservable()` when a signal should enter an RxJS pipeline. Use `toSignal()` when an observable's latest value should be read synchronously by Angular code or a template.

`toSignal()` subscribes immediately, so creating it repeatedly can duplicate side effects. Create it once and reuse it. Supply an `initialValue`, allow `undefined`, or use `requireSync: true` only for observables guaranteed to emit synchronously.

Signal reads after an `await` are not tracked by the reactive context because tracking is synchronous. Read needed signals before the asynchronous boundary.
keyPoints: Use signals for state; use RxJS for temporal orchestration.
Convert at stable boundaries instead of repeatedly switching abstractions.
`toSignal()` automatically cleans up with its injection context by default.
Use `untracked()` only for incidental reads, not to hide a circular state design.

blocks.title: Typeahead using a signal boundary and RxJS pipeline
blocks.explanation: The signal gives the template synchronous state. RxJS handles debounce, cancellation, errors, and asynchronous HTTP composition. The conversions occur once at a clear boundary.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Should signals replace RxJS in an Angular application?
blocks.answer:
No. Signals and RxJS overlap at the edges but have different strengths. I use signals for synchronous state, derived view models, inputs, and fine-grained template consumption. I use RxJS for events over time, HTTP cancellation, retries, rate limiting, concurrency, and multi-source asynchronous workflows.

I convert between them at feature boundaries using `toSignal()` or `toObservable()`. Replacing a clear RxJS pipeline with many effects usually makes cancellation and error behavior harder to understand.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer avoids the false “one technology wins” framing and explains ownership, time, cancellation, and lifecycle.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: An effect reads a signal and writes a new object back to the same signal on every run. What can happen?
blocks.answer:
The effect can repeatedly schedule itself because each write creates a new reference, which is unequal under the default `Object.is()` comparison. This can cause a loop, repeated synchronization, or unstable state.

The first fix is architectural: derive the value with `computed()` or update it only from an explicit event. Use `untracked()` only when a read is genuinely incidental and should not become a dependency. It should not be used to conceal a circular data flow.
blocks.explanation: The deeper lesson is that effects are side-effect boundaries, not a general state-propagation mechanism.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A progress store uses signals, but large pages still rerender and some effects loop. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
Keep one private writable source for each real domain state and expose read-only signals. Replace effects that copy or reshape data with computed selectors. Give components narrow selectors—for example `progressFor(topicId)`—instead of one giant object that every component reads.

Update immutably so equality can detect changes. Avoid reconstructing all records when one topic changes. If repeated lookups are expensive, store normalized data by ID and compute only the needed slice.

Reserve effects for persistence, telemetry, or imperative libraries. Register cleanup with the effect's `onCleanup` callback when it starts timers or external work. Inspect effects for service methods that read hidden signals; use explicit inputs or a carefully scoped `untracked()` read.

If API synchronization needs debounce, cancellation, retry, or ordering, cross into RxJS once, handle the stream there, and convert the latest result back to a signal. Validate with Angular DevTools and tests that count selector/effect executions.
blocks.explanation: This design reduces broad invalidation and makes source state, derivation, and side effects visibly different.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `effect()` to calculate derived state or calling `toSignal()` repeatedly inside a computed function or getter.
blocks.whyItHappens: Effects look convenient for reacting to values, and repeated conversion looks local, but it creates unnecessary subscriptions, circular writes, and unclear ownership.
blocks.correctApproach: Use `computed()` for pure derivation, create `toSignal()` once in an injection context, and keep effects only for synchronization with non-signal systems.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Design signal state as a small dependency graph: clear writable sources, pure computed values, narrow consumers, and a few explicit side-effect boundaries.
keyPoints: Expose read-only signals from stores and mutate through named domain commands.
Prefer normalized state and narrow computed selectors for large collections.
Use effect cleanup for timers and imperative integrations.
Do not use deep equality by default on large structures; it can cost more than the avoided update.
Test rapid updates, errors, teardown, and async-boundary behavior.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Signal = source/current value; computed = pure derived value; effect = external side effect.
- Signals and RxJS complement each other.
- Create interop conversions once and respect their subscription lifecycle.
- Avoid in-place mutation and circular effects.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/signals
- https://angular.dev/guide/signals/effect
- https://angular.dev/ecosystem/rxjs-interop
- https://angular.dev/api/core/untracked

title: RxJS switchMap vs mergeMap
description: RxJS flattening operators, request cancellation, race conditions, ordered work, duplicate-submit protection, and idempotency.

blocks.title: One question selects the flattening operator
blocks.content:
Flattening operators answer one question: when a new outer value arrives while earlier inner work is still running, what should happen?

- `switchMap`: stop listening to the previous inner observable and switch to the newest. Best for latest-only reads such as typeahead.
- `mergeMap`: keep multiple inner observables active concurrently. Best for independent work where every result matters; concurrency can be limited.
- `concatMap`: queue inner observables and run them one at a time in source order. Best for ordered writes.
- `exhaustMap`: ignore new outer values while the current inner observable is active. Best for guarding one in-flight submit or login attempt.

“Cancellation” means RxJS unsubscribes from the previous inner observable. Angular `HttpClient` will abort the client request when possible, but a server may already have received and processed it. Never rely on client cancellation as transactional protection.
keyPoints: Choose by concurrency policy, not by operator popularity.
Reads often fit switchMap; writes require business-specific idempotency and ordering.
mergeMap can overload APIs without a concurrency limit.
exhaustMap prevents repeated UI triggers only while the inner observable remains active.

blocks.title: Loading, errors, and teardown belong inside the active request
blocks.content:
A production pipeline must keep loading and error state tied to the correct inner request. Placing `catchError` outside `switchMap` can terminate the complete search stream after one failure. Placing it inside lets later user input continue to work.

Likewise, `finalize()` inside the inner observable belongs to that request, but a boolean loading flag can flicker if multiple requests overlap. Model request state as data or use an active-request counter when concurrency is allowed.

`distinctUntilChanged()` compares adjacent values with `===` by default. For filter objects, create a stable serialized query, use a meaningful comparator, or build the stream from individual fields.
keyPoints: Put recoverable request errors inside the inner pipeline.
Test delayed responses in the wrong order.
Disable or guard UI actions, but also enforce server-side idempotency for important writes.
Use marble tests or controlled schedulers for time and concurrency behavior.

blocks.title: Latest-only search with complete request state
blocks.explanation: Each query owns its own loading/success/error sequence. `switchMap` removes stale inner subscriptions, and `refCount` avoids keeping the feature stream alive after all consumers leave.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why is `switchMap` generally preferred for typeahead search?
blocks.answer:
A newer query makes an older query irrelevant. `switchMap` unsubscribes from the previous HTTP observable and listens only to the latest one, preventing a slow old response from replacing newer results.

I would also debounce only as much as user experience permits, ignore unchanged queries, handle errors inside the inner observable, and test out-of-order responses. The server should still tolerate aborted requests.
blocks.explanation: The important phrase is “latest result wins,” not merely “it cancels API calls.”

blocks.title: Operator choice
blocks.question: Which operator would you choose for duplicate submit, ordered autosave, and parallel file upload?
blocks.answer:
Duplicate submit: `exhaustMap` can ignore extra clicks while one request is active, plus disable the button and use a server idempotency key.

Ordered autosave: `concatMap` when each write must complete in order. If only the newest draft matters and the API is designed for replacement, a different latest-only strategy may be valid.

Parallel uploads: `mergeMap(file => upload(file), concurrency)` so every file is processed without opening unlimited connections.
blocks.explanation: There is no universal “best” flattening operator; the required concurrency semantics choose it.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A payment submission uses `switchMap`. Users occasionally see cancelled UI requests but duplicate payments on the backend. What is wrong?
blocks.answer:
`switchMap` is unsafe for a command that must complete exactly once. Unsubscribing from the client request does not undo work already accepted by the server. A second click can start another POST while the first payment is still being processed.

At the UI layer, use `exhaustMap` to ignore repeated clicks while the first request is active and visibly disable the action. At the API layer, require a stable idempotency key tied to the payment command, enforce uniqueness transactionally, and return the previous result when the same key is retried.

Handle uncertainty: if the network times out after the server accepted payment, query payment status by command ID rather than blindly posting again. Test double-clicks, retries, timeouts, browser refresh, and delayed responses.
blocks.explanation: RxJS controls client concurrency; correctness for money or orders must be guaranteed by the server and data store.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Choosing `switchMap` for every HTTP call because it is described as the “safe” operator.
blocks.whyItHappens: It solves stale latest-only reads, but it can discard required work or hide the result of a write that the server already processed.
blocks.correctApproach: Define whether new work should replace, join, queue, or be ignored. Then choose switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, or exhaustMap and add server guarantees where required.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Write the concurrency rule in plain English before writing the pipeline. The operator should make that rule obvious during code review.
keyPoints: Use `mergeMap` concurrency limits for bounded parallelism.
Put recoverable errors inside the inner observable so the outer UI stream stays alive.
Avoid unbounded `shareReplay`; define buffer, refCount, completion, and reset behavior.
Use `takeUntilDestroyed()` for long-lived manual subscriptions.
Test with controlled delays, cancellation, repeated clicks, and backend failures.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- switchMap = replace; mergeMap = parallel; concatMap = queue; exhaustMap = ignore while busy.
- Client unsubscription is not a server transaction rollback.
- Keep loading/error state attached to the active inner operation.
- Important commands need server idempotency.

Official references

- https://rxjs.dev/api/operators/switchMap
- https://rxjs.dev/api/operators/mergeMap
- https://rxjs.dev/api/operators/concatMap
- https://rxjs.dev/api/operators/exhaustMap
- https://angular.dev/guide/http/making-requests

title: HTTP Interceptors
description: Functional HTTP interceptors, immutable requests, request context, token refresh, retry safety, and security boundaries.

blocks.title: Interceptors as HTTP middleware
blocks.content:
An HTTP interceptor sits in Angular's `HttpClient` pipeline. It can inspect an outgoing request, clone it with changes, observe response events, transform errors, retry, cache, or return a synthetic response.

Angular supports functional and DI-based interceptors. The Angular team recommends functional interceptors because their behavior and ordering are more predictable in complex configurations.

Most `HttpRequest` and `HttpResponse` properties are immutable. Methods such as `headers.set()` return a new value; they do not mutate the original. Clone the request before forwarding it.

Interceptors form a chain in registration order. Request handling moves forward through that order; response observable behavior unwinds through the chain. Keep each interceptor focused so ordering remains understandable.
keyPoints: Register functional interceptors with `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))`.
Use `inject()` inside a functional interceptor to access services from its registration injector.
Clone immutable requests; take special care with deeply mutable bodies during retries.
Use `HttpContextToken` for per-request behavior such as skipping auth or caching.

blocks.title: Authentication refresh without loops
keyPoints: A shared in-flight refresh observable must reset after completion or error.
Add a request context marker to prevent refresh/retry loops.
Logout during refresh and multiple-tab behavior need explicit design.
Never put authorization decisions only in the client; the server is authoritative.

blocks.title: Focused auth interceptor with retry marker
blocks.explanation: The interceptor retries at most once and adds the newly returned token. `refreshOnce()` must implement single-flight sharing and reset its internal reference in `finalize()`. Non-idempotent calls still require API-level replay safety.

blocks.title: Immutability question
blocks.question: What happens if code calls `req.headers.set("X-Trace", id); next(req);` without assigning the returned headers or cloning the request?
blocks.answer: The outgoing request does not contain the new header. `HttpHeaders.set()` returns a new immutable `HttpHeaders` instance. The interceptor must pass a cloned request, for example `next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { "X-Trace": id } }))`.
blocks.explanation: This design makes retries and chained interceptors easier to reason about, but request bodies can still be deeply mutable and must be handled carefully.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What are good and bad responsibilities for an HTTP interceptor?
blocks.answer:
Good cross-cutting responsibilities include authentication headers, correlation IDs, standardized timing/telemetry, per-request caching policy, and normalization of transport-level errors.

Bad responsibilities include feature-specific business decisions, silently swallowing all errors, showing duplicate UI notifications for every request, retrying non-idempotent operations blindly, or mutating arbitrary response bodies. Keep business workflows in feature services where intent and user context are visible.
blocks.explanation: An interceptor should stay infrastructure-focused and predictable across every request that passes through it.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Five requests receive 401 together. The application starts five refresh calls, rotates the refresh token repeatedly, and logs the user out. How do you fix and test it?
blocks.answer:
Move refresh coordination into one session service. If a refresh is already active, return the same shared observable to every caller. If not, create the refresh request, share its single result, and clear the in-flight reference in `finalize()`.

The interceptor should exclude the refresh endpoint, mark an original request after one retry, and clone the retry with the fresh token. A failed refresh should transition the session to logged out exactly once and fail all waiting requests.

Do not replay unsafe POST operations automatically unless they carry an idempotency key and the server guarantees duplicate handling. For an uncertain command, query status instead.

Test simultaneous 401s, refresh success, refresh failure, a second 401 after retry, logout during refresh, slow responses, token rotation, multiple tabs, and requests configured to skip authentication. Assert exactly one refresh network call and no retry loop.
blocks.explanation: The core solution is single-flight coordination plus bounded, security-aware replay.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Putting every HTTP error into one global interceptor that retries and shows a toast.
blocks.whyItHappens: The interceptor lacks business context. It can retry unsafe writes, duplicate user messages, hide recoverable feature errors, and create loops.
blocks.correctApproach: Handle transport-wide concerns centrally, but let feature services/components decide business recovery and user messaging. Retry only explicitly safe operations with bounded policies.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Treat the interceptor chain as infrastructure code: small functions, explicit order, request-context controls, bounded retries, and security-focused tests.
keyPoints: Use correlation IDs and timing without logging sensitive headers or bodies.
Use `HttpContextToken` instead of URL string hacks for opt-in/opt-out behavior.
Make request transformations idempotent because retries may run the chain again.
Test with `HttpTestingController` and assert order, headers, retry count, and failure behavior.
Protect tokens, CSRF boundaries, redirects, and logout transitions according to the chosen auth architecture.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Functional interceptors are the recommended Angular style.
- Requests are immutable; clone them to change headers, params, URL, or context.
- Token refresh must be single-flight, bounded, and loop-safe.
- Client retry of important commands requires server idempotency.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/guide/http/interceptors
- https://angular.dev/guide/http/testing
- https://angular.dev/api/common/http/HttpContextToken
- https://angular.dev/guide/http/setup

title: Optimizing Change Detection for Large Dashboards
description: End-to-end performance design for high-frequency Angular dashboards with granular state, batching, virtualization, charts, and profiling.

blocks.title: Performance is a pipeline, not one Angular setting
keyPoints: Measure network, CPU, change detection, DOM, layout/paint, and memory separately.
Do not render every backend event if users cannot perceive that frequency.
Stable entity references and narrow selectors prevent unrelated widgets from updating.
Chart libraries often dominate cost even after Angular work is optimized.

blocks.title: A practical layered strategy
blocks.content:
Start upstream. Ask whether the server can aggregate, sample, or send deltas rather than full snapshots. Parse and normalize messages once in a feature service or worker.

Batch visual updates with an operator such as `bufferTime`, `auditTime`, or frame-aligned scheduling. The exact operator depends on whether the UI needs the latest value, all events, or periodic aggregates.

Store data by stable ID. Update only changed entities and expose a per-widget signal or selector. Avoid one `dashboardState()` object read by every widget if any update replaces the complete object.

For lists, use `@for (...; track widget.id)`. For large off-screen sets, use CDK virtual scrolling, pagination, tabs, collapse, or `@defer`. For charts, update series incrementally where supported and destroy charts when inactive.

Move CPU-heavy calculations that do not touch the DOM to a Web Worker only after profiling shows main-thread computation is the bottleneck. A worker adds serialization and coordination cost.
keyPoints: Batching trades freshness for responsiveness; define an acceptable UI update rate.
Virtualization reduces DOM but changes accessibility, keyboard, and measurement behavior that must be tested.
Workers help CPU work, not DOM or chart rendering.
Performance budgets should include interaction latency and memory, not only bundle size.

blocks.title: Batch once and update only affected widgets
blocks.explanation: The socket is consumed once, updates are batched, and widgets read only their own entity. In a very large map, further partitioning may be needed because replacing the map still invalidates computed reads of the map signal; profile and choose a more granular store if that becomes hot.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: A WebSocket sends 50 updates per second across 300 widgets. What would you optimize first?
blocks.answer:
I would first profile and inspect the update contract. If the server sends full dashboard snapshots, reduce that to deltas or aggregated updates. Then ingest once, batch visual updates to an acceptable rate, normalize by widget ID, and route only changed slices to their consumers.

Next I would measure chart redraws, DOM size, layout/paint, and selector allocations. I would virtualize or defer invisible widgets, use stable tracking, update chart data incrementally, and move proven CPU-heavy aggregation off the main thread. I would validate with interaction latency, long-task count, frame rate, memory, and dropped-message behavior.
blocks.explanation: The priority is reducing work at the source and narrowing invalidation, not sprinkling manual change-detection calls across 300 components.

blocks.title: NgZone question
blocks.question: What role does `NgZone.runOutsideAngular()` have in an Angular 22 dashboard?
blocks.answer:
Angular 22 is zoneless by default, so `runOutsideAngular()` is not needed to prevent ZoneJS from triggering change detection in a normal new application.

It can still matter in a library that supports both ZoneJS and zoneless applications, or in an application that explicitly opted back into `provideZoneChangeDetection()`. In that case, high-frequency setup can run outside the zone and publish a batched signal or call `markForCheck()` only when the UI should update.

The main optimization remains batching and granular state. `runOutsideAngular()` does not make expensive calculations or DOM updates free.
blocks.explanation: This corrects the older assumption that every Angular application automatically uses ZoneJS.

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: After batching WebSocket updates, the dashboard still freezes for 400 ms every second. How would you continue the investigation?
blocks.answer:
Record a performance trace around the freeze and inspect the longest tasks. If JavaScript is dominant, identify whether parsing, sorting, aggregation, cloning, or chart data transformation causes the spike. Split work across frames, incrementally update data, or move a pure heavy calculation to a worker.

If style/layout/paint dominates, inspect forced synchronous layout, chart canvas/SVG redraws, large DOM trees, sticky elements, shadows, and resize observers. Reduce rendered widgets, avoid read/write layout thrashing, and update only changed chart series.

Use memory tools to check whether old chart instances or datasets accumulate. Inspect garbage-collection pauses caused by rebuilding huge arrays and objects every batch. Preserve stable references and reuse buffers where safe.

Compare one optimization at a time using the same trace. The acceptance target should be explicit—for example no task over 50 ms during normal interaction, a stable heap after repeated navigation, and an agreed visual update latency.
blocks.explanation: Batching controls frequency, but each batch may still contain too much work. The trace determines the next layer to fix.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Subscribing to the same broad real-time stream in every widget and rebuilding complete dashboard arrays for each message.
blocks.whyItHappens: It looks locally simple, but it multiplies filtering, allocations, subscription work, and invalidation across the full widget count.
blocks.correctApproach: Ingest once, normalize centrally, update only changed entities, expose narrow selectors, batch render updates, and keep stable references for unaffected widgets.

blocks.title: Production guidance and validation
blocks.content: Set a dashboard performance contract and validate it on realistic hardware and data volume. Optimizations should have before/after evidence.
keyPoints: Track INP or task-specific interaction latency, long tasks, frame rate, memory, and message-to-paint delay.
Test slow devices, background/foreground transitions, reconnection bursts, and partial data loss.
Add virtual-scroll and keyboard/accessibility tests for large collections.
Destroy inactive charts, observers, sockets, and worker resources.
Use bundle analysis and `@defer` for heavy optional widgets, but measure route and interaction cost separately.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Angular 22 already defaults to OnPush and zoneless behavior.
- Reduce message volume, batch rendering, normalize state, and narrow consumers.
- Profile chart/DOM/layout work and memory, not only Angular checks.
- Use virtualization, deferral, workers, and server aggregation only for measured bottlenecks.

Official references

- https://angular.dev/best-practices/runtime-performance
- https://angular.dev/guide/zoneless
- https://angular.dev/guide/templates/defer
- https://angular.dev/tools/devtools
- https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp
